title: Launching on X: Build in Public, the Nabulines Way

scenes.narration: Welcome to Nabulines Academy. In this lesson, you're going to learn how to announce your work on X — formerly Twitter — in a way that actually gets attention. Not spam. Not begging for followers. Real, honest sharing that makes people want to try what you built. Let's dive in.

visual.title: Launching on X
visual.subtitle: Build in Public, the Nabulines Way

scenes.narration: First: what does 'build in public' mean? It means you share your work *while you're making it* — not just the polished final product. You show the messy middle. The bugs. The small wins. The 'I just figured out how to make this work' moments. Why? Because people connect with the journey, not just the destination. When you share your process, you're not selling — you're inviting people to watch you grow. And that earns trust way faster than a slick marketing pitch.

visual.title: What 'Build in Public' Means
bullets: Share the journey, not just the finish line
Show the messy middle — bugs, breakthroughs, learning
People connect with real progress
Builds trust faster than polished marketing

scenes.narration: So how do you actually write a launch post? Start with a *hook* — one sentence that makes someone stop scrolling. Not 'I built a thing.' That's boring. Try: 'I spent 3 days fighting CSS and finally made a tool that does X in one click.' Or: 'Here's the dumbest bug that taught me the most.' The hook is the promise — it tells people why they should care. Then, in the next sentence or two, explain *what* you built and *who it's for*. Be specific. 'A tool for designers' is vague. 'A color palette generator that exports to Figma' — that's clear.

visual.title: Anatomy of a Launch Post
bullets: Hook: one sentence that stops the scroll
What: explain the tool in plain language
Who: be specific about who it helps
Why: the problem it solves
Link: make it easy to try

scenes.narration: Next: tell them *why* you built it. What problem were you solving? Even if the problem is small — 'I got tired of manually doing X' — that's real. People trust real problems. Then, and this is key: *link to the thing*. Don't make them hunt for it. Put the URL right in the post. If it's live on Cloudflare Pages, paste that pages-dot-dev link. If it's a GitHub repo, link that. Make it one click away. And if you have a screenshot or a short video, attach it. Visuals get way more engagement than text alone.

visual.title: Make It Easy to Try
bullets: State the problem you solved (even if small)
Link directly — no hunting required
Attach a screenshot or demo video
Visuals = more engagement

scenes.narration: Here's an example. 'I built a markdown-to-HTML converter because I was tired of copy-pasting into WordPress. It's live at my-tool-dot-pages-dot-dev — try it and let me know what breaks.' That's it. Hook, what, why, link. No fluff. No 'please retweet' begging. Just: here's a thing, here's why I made it, go try it. That honesty is what makes people click. And when they do try it and it works? They'll tell others. That's how you grow an audience — one real person at a time.

visual.title: Example Launch Post
bullets: 'I built a markdown-to-HTML converter…'
'…because I was tired of copy-pasting into WordPress.'
'It's live at my-tool.pages.dev — try it.'
Hook + what + why + link = done

scenes.narration: A few don'ts. Don't overhype. Don't say 'game-changer' or 'revolutionary' unless it actually is. Don't apologize — 'sorry it's not perfect' makes people expect it to be bad. And don't ghost after you post. If someone replies with feedback or a question, answer them. That interaction is how you turn a post into a conversation, and a conversation into a community. Building in public isn't just about announcing — it's about *engaging*.

visual.title: What NOT to Do
bullets: Don't overhype ('game-changer' unless it is)
Don't apologize ('sorry it's not perfect')
Don't ghost — reply to feedback
Building in public = engaging, not just posting

scenes.narration: One more thing: consistency beats virality. You don't need one post to blow up. You need to keep sharing. Every small win. Every lesson learned. Every new feature. Over time, people start to recognize your name. They see you're actually building, not just talking. And that's when the trust compounds. So post your launch today. Then post again tomorrow about the first bug someone found. Then post next week about the fix. That's the Nabulines way — show up, share the work, and let the results speak.

visual.title: Consistency Over Virality
bullets: One viral post < regular sharing
Every small win, every lesson, every feature
People recognize your name over time
Trust compounds with consistency

scenes.narration: Alright — you now know how to write a launch post that earns attention without feeling like spam. Your exercise: draft a real launch post for your tool. Write the hook, explain what it does, link to it, and post it. Don't wait for perfect. Post it today. In the next lesson, we're going to talk about how to handle feedback — the good, the bad, and the 'why doesn't this button work' — and turn it into fuel for your next build. See you there.

quiz.q: What is the first part of a good launch post?
options: A hook — one sentence that stops the scroll

quiz.q: Why should you link directly to your tool in the post?
options: To make people work for it
To make it one click away — no hunting
To test if people are interested

quiz.q: What matters more than one viral post?

exercise: Draft a launch post for your tool. Write a hook, explain what it does and who it's for, state the problem it solves, and include a direct link. Post it on X (or save it to post when your tool is live). Bonus: attach a screenshot or short demo video.
